title: What Everyone Is Missing About Ceuta
gist: Howard French argues that Ceuta — seized by Portugal in 1415 to capture African gold and inherited by Spain through a 1580 succession fluke — is a historical accident whose retention now costs Spain real money and European goodwill. His bet: demographics will force Spain to hand Ceuta back to Morocco and to lead a European rethink of migration, since Africa's population is growing fastest while Spanish and Italian fertility sits near one child per woman.

insights.claim: Portugal's 1415 seizure of Ceuta under the future Henry the Navigator was driven not by religious conversion or territory but by access to sub-Saharan gold flowing north through Mediterranean Africa — commerce, not crusade, launched European imperialism.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Reframes Europe's foundational wealth as extracted from Africa — the moral premise for French's argument that Europe owes Africa economic integration, not policing.
insights.quote: Rather, it was access to the huge wealth in gold that had flowed into Europe for centuries via Mediterranean Africa from points far to the south, below the Sahara Desert.
insights.locator: What Henry sought was not converts

insights.claim: Iberian expansion into Africa was deliberate strategy rather than accidental drift — the Canary Islands rivalry involved Portuguese slave raiding and a Spanish campaign against the Guanche that some historians consider the first modern genocide.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Rejecting the 'absence of mind' account of empire is what makes Spanish claims to Ceuta hard to defend as innocent inheritance.
insights.quote: it is a mistake to buy into the notion that Portugal acquired its imperial possessions in Africa as “in a fit of absence of mind”
insights.locator: As I wrote in my book, Born in Blackness

insights.claim: Ceuta became Spanish only through a chain of accidents: Sebastian I's death invading Morocco, the heirless Portuguese king Henry's death in 1580, Philip II's claim to the Portuguese crown, and the cession of Ceuta after Portugal restored its own royal line.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The legal title rests on a dynastic accident rather than settlement or Spanish conquest — weak historical ground when Morocco presses its claim.
insights.quote: This left Philip II of Spain, the grandson of a Portuguese king, with the strongest claim to the Portuguese crown upon Henry’s death in 1580.

insights.claim: Spain rejects Morocco's historic and geographic arguments for Ceuta while making nearly identical arguments against Britain over Gibraltar, an inconsistency that undermines Madrid's negotiating position.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The Ceuta-Gibraltar linkage is the diplomatic lever — any move on one reopens the other, which is why both have stayed frozen.
insights.quote: Spain rejects Morocco’s historic and geographic arguments to rightful ownership of Ceuta, but it makes very similar claims to Gibraltar.

insights.claim: Ceuta's status is a historical fluke that international recognition merely papers over, and one unlikely to endure.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A live sovereignty question on the EU's southern edge is an under-priced geopolitical variable for Spain-Morocco trade, energy and migration cooperation.
insights.quote: this situation is clearly a historical fluke, and one that seems unlikely to endure.
insights.locator: Although extended a patina of legitimacy

insights.claim: Keeping Ceuta delivers Spain nothing but imperial nostalgia while imposing large ongoing fiscal costs for policing against migrant surges plus recurring intra-European tensions.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The cost-benefit case for retention is negative on French's accounting, which is the mechanism by which he expects Spanish policy to flip.
insights.quote: policing Ceuta against the next upsurge in immigrants incurs large, ongoing fiscal costs and intra-European tensions.

insights.claim: Tens of thousands of Africans stormed Ceuta's beaches and most had returned within 48 hours, yet Europe's right-wing parties and press sensationalized the episode for political or commercial gain.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The gap between the event's actual duration and its political amplification shows migration headlines are a manufactured volatility source in European politics.
insights.quote: Though most had returned within 48 hours, Europe’s right-wing parties and press sensationalized what was happening for political or commercial gain
insights.locator: Indeed, last week, much of Europe recoiled

insights.claim: Italy responded to the Ceuta episode by screening arrivals from Spain, showing a single exclave incident can trigger internal European border fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Schengen integrity is now hostage to localized migration events — a recurring friction for European freight, travel and labor mobility.
insights.quote: Spain’s near-neighbor, Italy, quickly instituted the screening of people arriving from Spain to make sure that no Africans were sneaking in through Spain’s North African exclave.
insights.locator: Indeed, last week, much of Europe recoiled

insights.claim: European reaction to Ceuta reveals that continental public opinion is easily inflamed by any sudden foreign influx, especially one involving brown- and Black-skinned people.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Racialized reaction is a hard political constraint on rational migration policy in Europe regardless of the economic case.
insights.quote: public opinion on the continent is easily stirred by the prospect of any big and sudden foreign influx, especially one that involves brown- and Black-skinned people.
insights.locator: The quick and fierce lashing out against Spain

insights.claim: Africa's population is growing faster than any other region, though somewhat more slowly than projected a decade ago, while European fertility in countries including Spain and Italy has fallen to roughly one child per woman.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The demographic divergence makes migration pressure a permanent structural flow, not a series of crises — plan European labor supply and fiscal projections accordingly.
insights.quote: Europe is heading in the exact opposite direction, with women in many countries—including Spain and Italy, to take two southern European examples—having roughly one child on average.
insights.locator: The reason for that can be summed up

insights.claim: Spain has already granted amnesty to many previously illegal immigrants and publicly identified continued immigration as one of the rare available remedies for population collapse — the most clear-eyed European position on the trend.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Spain is the European test case for immigration-as-demographic-policy; its labor force and growth outcomes become the reference data for the continent.
insights.quote: granting amnesty to many who have immigrated illegally in the past, and hitherto publicly identifying continued immigration as one of the rare available remedies for population collapse
insights.locator: Spain’s government has taken the wisest measure

insights.claim: French's explicit bet is that Spain will gradually and perhaps soon abandon its African territorial claim out of a realism that Britain has failed to apply to Gibraltar.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A named, falsifiable forecast: Spanish cession of Ceuta would be a major Spain-Morocco reset, relevant to Moroccan sovereign risk, energy links and Spanish border spending.
insights.quote: My bet, though, is that Spain will gradually, and perhaps even soon, see the wisdom of abandoning its African territorial claim out of a realism that has so far eluded the British in Gibraltar.
insights.locator: My bet, though, is that Spain will gradually

insights.claim: Spain should return Ceuta to Morocco to close off its use as a backdoor into the Schengen zone, since the territory is geopolitically insignificant.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Sovereignty transfer framed as a border-control measure rather than a concession — the argument most likely to move Spanish domestic opinion.
insights.quote: At this point, Spain should do the right thing and restore this geopolitically insignificant territory to Morocco, closing off the possibility of it ever being used as a backdoor into the pan-European immigration zone known as Schengen.
insights.locator: At this point, Spain should do the right thing

insights.claim: Much of Europe holds the delusion that movement of people from Africa and the global south can be managed indefinitely through little more than police action, when migrants will keep arriving in ever larger numbers regardless.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Border-security spending is sized against a problem it cannot solve — expect continued policy failure and political instability from the enforcement-only approach.
insights.quote: But Africans and other migrants will continue to show up in Europe in ever larger numbers no matter what.
insights.locator: Much of the rest of Europe clings

insights.claim: The volume of future African migration to Europe depends on whether Europe renovates its economic ties with Africa today so prosperity spreads there — inverting the historical direction in which wealth once flowed from Africa to Europe.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Frames African development investment as European migration policy — the strongest argument for scaling EU-Africa trade and infrastructure capital.
insights.quote: Just how many, though, will depend on what Europe does today to renovate its economic ties to the continent just to the south, making sure that prosperity spreads there, as it once did from Africa to Europe.
insights.locator: Much of the rest of Europe clings
